newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo to invest $200mln to upgrade flight security.
newsitem.headline: Yugo to invest $200mln to upgrade flight security.

text.p: Yugoslavia intends to spend up to $200 million upgrading its air traffic control equipment over a five-year period, a senior Yugoslav Air Traffic Control Authority official said on Thursday.

"We are close to completing a master plan to replace everything that is not of sufficient quality, is technically outdated or is preventing us from joining European systems," Branko Bilbija, the director of the Authority, told reporters.
"For this we will seek a credit worth between $150 and $200 million," added Bilbija, a general of the Yugoslav Air Force.
He declined to specify if the funds were expected to be provided by domestic or foreign sources.
He said such big investments required serious planning and would be carried out in phases but he expected the air system's hardware to be completely renewed in five years.
The aim is to conform to European standards to harmonise and integrate flight control in Europe, Bilbija said.

Several air near-misses had occurred recently, according to reports in the media, but mistakes by the system had been ruled out. "I would not like to minimise events, one or two were a little more serious than others ... but it is impossible to completely rule out such incidents. This happens in the world, too," Bilbija said.
Air corridors above Yugoslavia were not closed during the international war-related 1992-96 sanctions against the country, but overflight charges were paid into blocked bank accounts.
Yugoslavia has recovered most of these funds, Bilbija said.
He said air traffic had been growing annually by five to 10 percent since 1992.

In 1990, before the breakup of ex-Yugoslavia, 170,000 aircraft flew over the former federation. "Now over 200,000 planes fly over the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (comprising only Serbia and Montenegro) every year. This figure excludes local military flights," he said.
There are up to 1,000 planes in Yugoslavia's airspace a day in the peak traffic period.

The director of the technical centre Colonel Boca Muncan said although the equipment of the flight control centre was purchased in the early eighties it was estimated to be 99.85 percent reliable by international standards.

Bilbija said that this year Belgrade had already made some additions to its flight control equipment. Two new radars have been installed, on Mts Kopaonik and Fruska Gora, which ensure "triple radar coverage" of Yugoslav airspace while only double coverage is required by international regulations.
Another project under way is upgrading Belgrade's Surcin international airport to category II. "Works began a month ago and we expect them to be completed by November 1," Bilbija said.
Total investment in the work is estimated to be up to $10 million, financed by the Federal Air Traffic Authority and the Belgrade airport company. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 311 4305
